Meeting header:
Date: 2026-12-03 15:30 UTC
Duration: ~92 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel (Redwood AE), Jonah Reyes (Redwood SE), Dr. Priya Nambiar (Redwood ML), Ravi Kaur (Redwood SRE); Ethan Ward (Apollo Head of ML), Lina Ortega (Apollo Platform), Marcus Li (Apollo CTO), Sofia Park (Apollo Data Eng)

Auto summary (auto-gen, may be rough):

Transcript: (timestamps approximate, transcription imperfect)

[00:00] Samira Patel: All right folks, thanks for joining. We'll kick off — we're targeting a deep dive on the 128k-plus workload and how the KV cache + eviction policies affect p95/p99. Jonah, wanna start with an overview?

[00:18] Jonah Reyes: Yeah, sure. Hi everyone. Quick topo: Redwood's runtime keeps a KV cache per request shard, and we do continuous batching across concurrent sessions. For really long contexts we rely on prefix caching plus "sparse eviction" when memory pressure hits. Today we want to show where the tradeoffs are — eviction frequency, recompute cost, and how that plays into latency SLOs.

[00:36] Ethan Ward: Quick clarifying Q — when you say "sparse eviction" are you talking about block-level eviction or whole-layer rollbacks?

[00:42] Jonah Reyes: Primarily block-level, we evict KV blocks (key/value chunk pairs) by recency and by importance heuristics. There's an optional pinned set for recent instructions. But there are cases where you'll see bursty recompute if the eviction threshold is too aggressive.

[00:58] Lina Ortega: We observed that with our 200k-ish transcripts some of the downstream tokens spike latency. We see like high variance at p99, p999. Trying to understand if it's network, or CPU/GPU recompute, or the cache misses.

[01:14] Dr. Priya Nambiar: Common pattern is a cache miss causes a KV repopulate which triggers a short spike due to KV materialization + attention recompute on layers that reference it. Two levers: prefetch via chunking or keep larger pinned segments at higher memory cost.

[01:35] Marcus Li: What's the memory profile? If we want pinned segments for the last 64k tokens, what are we looking at on say a 80GB GPU?

[01:41] Jonah Reyes: Good question. Roughly, for our base Llama-like 70B fp16 model, storing KV for 64k tokens is ~X GB — (note: transcript may garble numbers) — in practice we'd expect 40-50GB of KV. On an 80GB GPU that leaves limited headroom for activations and temporary buffers; quantization helps but changes latency characteristics.

[01:59] Ethan Ward: That "X GB" — can you put exact numbers in the follow-up? We need to map that to our Dedicated pool sizing.

[02:06] Samira Patel: Yes we'll send exact tables. Also important: quantization to int4/5 reduces memory but increases decode time slightly and may amplify recompute latency when KVs are restored.

[02:22] Sofia Park: Could you explain how quantization affect KV layout? Is it compressed on-GPU or streamed in compressed form?

[02:28] Jonah Reyes: We currently store KV in the memory format native to the kernel. For int4/int8 we have compressed storage with on-read expand. So on an eviction we pull compressed blocks and expand, which adds CPU/GPU overhead. That's why sometimes quantization helps price but adds p99 latency.

[02:49] [03:00] Lina Ortega: The other piece is network between control plane and VPC. If we do Private deployment there's some extra egress hops. How do you measure that?

[03:08] Ravi Kaur: For Redwood Private the control plane talk is minimized; inference traffic stays in customer VPC if configured. Network adds are usually small (<10ms) unless there's cross-region routing. We'll include network hop breakdown in the traces.

[03:22] Ethan Ward: Great. Wanted to dive into chunking strategies. We're experimenting with hierarchical chunking — sliding windows + summary embeddings. How would Redwood's runtime interact with that?

[03:32] Jonah Reyes: Chunking at the application layer is complementary. If you feed the runtime chunked prompts, the KV growth per request reduces. But then you lose some global attention unless you stitch attention externally or use selective cross-attention. We recommend a hybrid: keep full KV for the last N tokens, chunk older context and serve as condensed summaries (embeddings) with a rerank step.

[03:56] Marcus Li: Does that approach require model changes? Are you effectively relying on retrieval augmentation?

[04:02] Dr. Priya Nambiar: No model changes per se; it's more prompt engineering and retrieval. But for certain long-context architectures it's useful to have sparse attention kernels (block-sparse) to ensure that recompute on a chunk boundary doesn't blow up.

[04:18] [04:40] Lina Ortega: We also saw an odd pattern: when we use batching aggressively, p50 is great but p99 spikes with larger batch sizes. Is that expected?

[04:47] Jonah Reyes: Yes — batching helps amortize kernel launches but increases tail due to head-of-queue latency and straggler batches (one large request in a batch). Continuous batching reduces variance, but if you have variable-length decoding bursts, you get stragglers. We recommend adaptive batching: reduce batch depth for low-latency tiers and allow higher batch depth for throughput tiers.

[05:13] Ethan Ward: Can Redwood do priority preemption? Like reserve slots for low-latency flows?

[05:18] Samira Patel: Yes, Redwood Dedicated supports routing policies — you can tag requests by SLA and they get scheduled differently, including preemptive micro-slices. We'll demo preemption in the perf run.

[05:31] [06:00] Sofia Park: Let's talk eviction heuristics — LRU vs. frequency vs. importance. Our workload has lots of repeated instrument names, would LFU be better?

[06:08] Jonah Reyes: LFU can help on highly repetitive sequences; but LFU tends to keep cold-but-frequently-used old blocks which can hurt for recency-driven context. We often use a hybrid LRUF (LRU with frequency boost) and a pinned window for the most recent 8-16k tokens. That reduces recompute for conversational recency while still freeing space.

[06:33] Dr. Priya Nambiar: We also experiment with "semantic pinning" — note hot blocks based on attention weights, not just recency. That requires us to track per-key utility wrist — sorry per-key utility metrics which we do server-side. There's some compute overhead but big wins for doc-centric queries.

[06:58] Marcus Li: Does that metric collection add a lot of overhead?

[07:04] Jonah Reyes: Minimal at scale; we aggregate on a sampling basis (1-5% of tokens) and then approximate. The overhead is a few percent CPU/GPU, but helps p99 if your workload is semantic-heavy.

[07:20] [07:45] Lina Ortega: About persistent KV — we want to test persistent KV across requests (so the cache survives process restarts). Do you support that in Redwood Dedicated?

[07:53] Ravi Kaur: Yes, we have an experimental persistent KV layer that writes compressed KV to fast NVMe and can restore into GPU on demand. It's a trade: restore cost vs. warm start. For long-lived sessions it's efficient; for ephemeral requests you pay restoration latency.

[08:14] Ethan Ward: Any numbers on restore time for a 64k KV snapshot from NVMe to GPU?

[08:20] Jonah Reyes: On our testbed NVMe with 3.5 GB/s sustained, a 40GB snapshot compressed to ~12GB (int4) takes ~3-5 seconds to bring into memory; with streaming restoration you can start low-latency decode and stream missing KV which reduces perceived latency but adds complexity. We'll provide measured numbers in follow-up.

[08:42] [09:10] Marcus Li: That 3-5s seems big. For us some flows are interactive and can't tolerate seconds. What are mitigations?

[09:17] Dr. Priya Nambiar: Mitigations: incremental restore (hot prefixes first), pre-warming predicted sessions, keeping small pinned windows, and summary-based fallbacks. Also load balancing across instances with warm caches.

[09:34] Lina Ortega: Let's discuss quantization again — we've seen quantization to int4 gives good cost wins but unpredictably worse p99 under KV restore. Any specific guidance?

[09:44] Jonah Reyes: If you quantize KVs, your expand code path becomes a bottleneck on restore. For Dedicated we recommend keeping KVs in int8 or fp16 for very latency-sensitive tiers and use int4/int5 for cold storage. Another pattern: keep most recent 8-16k in higher precision, quantize older blocks.

[10:08] [10:40] Sofia Park: How about offloading KV to CPU host memory? Is that practical for 128k contexts?

[10:47] Ravi Kaur: Offload to host memory is possible but you pay PCIe/GPUDirect transfer latency. For extremely large contexts you can shard KV across multiple GPUs (runtime sharding) and serve parts of the context from remote devices — but that requires careful placement to keep p99 reasonable.

[11:09] Ethan Ward: Could you explain runtime sharding? We saw a mention of sharding in a benchmark doc but not clear.

[11:15] Jonah Reyes: Runtime sharding slices the KV and model state across GPUs either by layer or by token ranges. For long-context reads we can localize the hot zone on a single GPU and keep cold ranges remote. That reduces per-GPU memory but introduces network fetch latencies between GPUs — typically microseconds to low ms depending on NVLink vs. ethernet.

[11:39] [12:00] Marcus Li: If we do cross-GPU fetches, do you compress across the wire?

[12:06] Jonah Reyes: Yes we stream compressed blocks and decompress on arrival. Our protocol supports delta encoding to reduce repeated transmission.

[12:18] Lina Ortega: Let's talk observability — what traces will you provide from the perf run?

[12:23] Samira Patel: We'll provide token-level latency traces, KV hit/miss timelines, per-layer recompute counts, and network hop latencies. Also a heatmap of eviction events aggregated by token index. Expect CSV + interactive dashboard link.

[12:40] [13:00] Sofia Park: Great. For the perf run we want to replicate our production concurrency pattern: mostly long tails with intermittent short queries. Can you replicate that in Dedicated?

[13:07] Ravi Kaur: Yes — we'll run synthetic clients that mirror your concurrency, plus a copy of your prompt set. We can also run stress tests for heavy retraining/finetune-like attention patterns.

[13:23] Ethan Ward: On security side: our compliance team wants assurance around NVMe persistence and KMS integration. We'll need to see the security pack.

[13:30] Samira Patel: We'll send the security pack (SOC2/ISO details, NVMe encryption, KMS integration guide). For VPC/on-prem we have options to keep control plane metadata encrypted and out of logs.

[13:46] [14:10] Marcus Li: Are there differences in behavior between Hosted API and Dedicated for KV eviction?

[14:15] Jonah Reyes: The runtime is the same codebase but Dedicated lets you tune memory thresholds, pinned window size, and persistent KV options. Hosted is optimized for multi-tenant fairness; Dedicated is much more configurable for local caching/pinning and preemption.

[14:32] Lina Ortega: One edge case: our workflows sometimes do long random-access reads into an old transcript (not sequential). How does that affect caching?

[14:40] Dr. Priya Nambiar: Random-access patterns cause high miss rates; better to prefetch predicted windows or to materialize condensed representations for rare lookups. Also consider storing embeddings for sections and use retrieval to reduce raw KV pressure.

[14:56] [15:30] Jonah Reyes: Quick demo idea: in the perf run we can instrument a scenario where we intentionally force eviction pressure and show the delta in p99 with and without semantic pinning. That usually convinces platform teams.

[15:42] Ethan Ward: Yes please. Also include a variant with int8 KVs vs int4 cold store.

[15:50] Samira Patel: Noted. We'll include the 3 variants: high-precision pinned window, hybrid quantized, and aggressive quantize+restore pattern.

[16:04] Lina Ortega: What about RPC timeouts? If restore takes multiple seconds, do you fallback to a condensed summary?

[16:11] Jonah Reyes: We have fallback policies: summary fallback, partial decode (streaming missing KV), and graceful degrade to smaller context window. Those are configurable per route.

[16:24] Marcus Li: Anything else around batching? Do you support dynamic batching windows?

[16:30] Ravi Kaur: Yes dynamic batching with latency targets: the runtime will tune batch width to meet configured latency SLOs. For Dedicated we can set strict p95/p99 targets that'll bias scheduling towards lower batch depth.

[16:44] [17:00] Sofia Park: Would love to see a sample configuration file showing these knobs.

[17:05] Samira Patel: We'll include a sample Dedicated config with pinned_window_k, eviction_policy, batch_depth targets, and restore thresholds.

[17:16] Ethan Ward: On the subject of VPC/on-prem: we have an air-gapped requirement for some datasets. Can Redwood run in air-gapped mode?

[17:23] Samira Patel: Yes, Redwood Private has an air-gapped deployment option; note that updates and telemetry require explicit approval. There's a packaging window for on-prem install and special licensing. We'll include that in the security doc.

[17:34] Lina Ortega: Ok, let's summarize the perf run specifics so we can schedule.

[17:40] Jonah Reyes: Proposed perf run: 2 hours on Dedicated pool (4 GPUs equivalent), three variants (high-precision pinned, hybrid quantized, aggressive quantize+restore), workload: your 128k prompt set + background concurrency pattern. Metrics: p50/p95/p99/p999, KV hit/miss, restore times, network latencies, batch depth stats.

[17:59] Marcus Li: Sounds good. Who will provision?

[18:03] Ravi Kaur: We'll provision and share access; ETA 2026-12-12. We asked Ethan to share the sample prompts and expected concurrency by 2026-12-09.

[18:14] Ethan Ward: Confirmed. We'll get that out.

[18:18] [18:45] Dr. Priya Nambiar: One optional experiment: test runtime sharding across two nodes with NVLink vs network and compare p99. That gives you a sense of cross-GPU fetch costs.

[18:28] Jonah Reyes: We'll add that as bonus.

[18:32] Lina Ortega: A couple last quick questions — licensing for Dedicated perf runs? Any extra cost?

[18:37] Samira Patel: This initial perf run is part of the pilot program; full Dedicated capacity would be priced as reserved capacity. We'll send pricing options; no surprises for the perf test.

[18:45] [19:10] Sofia Park: Closing question: in your past tests, what's typical p99 delta moving from 64k -> 128k pinned window?

[19:17] Jonah Reyes: It depends a lot on workload. For sequential accesses with pinned windows it's often a modest increase (20-40% p99 increase) but for high-randomness it's bigger. The key is the eviction policy and hot-set pinning. We'll quantify with your data.

[19:33] Ethan Ward: Great. Any blockers?

[19:36] Samira Patel: None from Redwood; main blockers are Apollo providing the prompt set and approving the Dedicated window.
